title: The number ONE river guide!
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
prayer: Lord, I take the cup of salvation and call upon your name. Let receiving you change the way I live. Give me a heart that produces good fruit and the courage not merely to hear your words but to act upon them. When I wander onto another road, call me back. When the waters rise, remind me where my foundation lies. And as you lead me home, keep my eyes open to all the beauty you have placed along the way. Amen.
body:
Currently, the Church is reading through 1 Corinthians, and I find myself imagining Paul trying to settle this young Christian community into an entirely new way of living. These are new sheep learning where they belong and how they are supposed to live now that they know and believe in Jesus.

Paul warns them about idolatry, but then he says something profound: “The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the Blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the Body of Christ?” If we participate in the Body and Blood of Christ, how can we then knowingly participate in something opposed to him? Paul even asks, “So what am I saying? That meat sacrificed to idols is anything? Or that an idol is anything?” The idol itself is nothing. The deeper question is what we have chosen to participate in and to whom we have given ourselves.

Then Psalm 116 asks a remarkably simple question: “How shall I make a return to the Lord for all the good he has done for me?” And the answer comes: “The cup of salvation I will take up, and I will call upon the name of the Lord.”

What a wonderful invitation. God has given us so much, and our response begins by reaching toward him. Take the cup. Call upon his name. Receive what he is offering.

Then Jesus takes this one step further in Luke. A good tree produces good fruit. A bad tree produces bad fruit. The fruit reveals something about the tree because eventually what is inside must make its way outside. Jesus says the same thing about us: “A good person out of the store of goodness in his heart produces good.” What fills the heart eventually becomes visible in the life.

And then Jesus asks a question that almost interrupts the simplicity of everything that came before it: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ but not do what I command?”

There it is.

It is not enough simply to hear. It is not enough simply to know. And perhaps it is not enough to receive Christ at the altar if receiving him never changes what happens when we leave it.

Jesus describes the person who hears his words **and acts on them** as someone building a house. This person digs deeply and places the foundation upon rock. The river eventually comes, the flood crashes against the house, and yet the house remains because of what lies beneath it. Another person hears exactly the same words but does nothing with them. His house has no foundation. When the river comes, it collapses.

Both people heard Jesus.

Only one acted.

Maybe that is the invitation running through all of today's readings. Take the cup of Christ. Receive the Body of Christ. Call upon the name of the Lord. But then **live as someone who has received him.**

And perhaps there is also a call here to return.

Not someday. Not when life settles down. Not when we are older, wiser, less busy, more certain, or somehow finally worthy. Look at the road you are traveling right now. If there are no signs pointing toward Christ, perhaps it is time to turn around.

And for those already traveling toward him, there will still be detours. We will miss turns. Something interesting will catch our attention and away we go. Sometimes we may travel quite a distance before realizing we have wandered from the road.

But we have a guide.

Maybe Christ is our Captain, our river guide, our pilot, our tour guide—the one who can see farther down the road than we possibly can. And if we allow him to lead, perhaps we begin to understand that following him does not mean missing everything beautiful along the way.

Quite the opposite.

Maybe he is the one who knows exactly where to stop for the sunset. He knows when the meteor shower will cross the sky. He knows where the elusive bird will appear, where the hidden lake lies beyond the trees, where the flower somehow grows in the desert, and when to become still enough to notice the zephyr passing across our face.

We spend so much of life afraid that following God will make us miss something.

Perhaps we have it backwards.

Follow him, and we may finally begin to notice what we have been missing all along.
